The withdrawal amount is deducted from the staking manager's balance externally, but the Validator.balance field remains unchanged, creating a state inconsistency between the on-chain validator record and actual staked balance. This causes future performance scoring and rebalancing decisions to be based on incorrect balance data.

extra_findings.title: Performance Update Overwrites Validator State Without Preserving Active Flag
extra_findings.description: In updateValidatorPerformance, the validator struct is overwritten using a memory struct that explicitly sets active: _validators[index].active. However, this is redundant and misleading — the active flag is read from storage and written back, but if the storage value were corrupted or the read failed, the write would still proceed. More critically, the function does not validate that the validator is active before updating performance, relying on the validatorActive modifier. However, the modifier is applied to the external function, but the internal write uses _validators[index].active which is read from storage. If the validator was deactivated between modifier check and storage write (e.g., via reentrancy), the active flag could be overwritten to false even if the validator was active at modifier check time. This creates a race condition where a malicious actor can deactivate a validator by triggering a performance update during a reentrant call to deactivateValidator.

extra_findings.title: Delegation Validation Bypass via Non-Active Validator
extra_findings.description: The getDelegation function requires the delegated validator to be active via validatorActiveState(validator). However, the setDelegation function only requires the validator to be active at the time of setting. If a validator is later deactivated, getDelegation will revert, but the delegation mapping still points to an inactive validator. This is not a direct vulnerability, but it creates a dangerous state where a staking manager's delegation target becomes unusable without any mechanism to auto-reset or notify. However, the real issue is in the logic of setDelegation: it allows setting a delegation to a validator that is currently inactive, and only later validation in getDelegation prevents usage. This creates a window where a manager can set a delegation to a validator they plan to deactivate, effectively locking the staking manager into a dead end. This is a lifecycle integrity flaw because the system allows state transitions that lead to unrecoverable deadlocks.

extra_findings.title: Rebalance Request Addition Allows Duplicate Requests via Reentrancy
extra_findings.description: The _addRebalanceRequest function checks !_validatorsWithPendingRebalance.contains(validator) before adding a request. However, this check and the subsequent add() are not atomic. If an attacker calls rebalanceWithdrawal with a validator address, and during the external call to IStakingManager.processValidatorWithdrawals, a reentrant call to rebalanceWithdrawal is made with the same validator, the second call will pass the contains check because the first add() has not yet completed. This allows multiple rebalance requests for the same validator to be created, leading to double withdrawal of funds. The vulnerability exists because the function does not use a mutex or reentrancy guard on the internal _addRebalanceRequest, and the external call to IStakingManager may trigger reentrancy.

extra_findings.title: Validator Index Mapping Corruption via Array Manipulation
extra_findings.description: The _validators array is manipulated via push() and never shrunk. When a validator is deactivated, its entry in _validators is not removed — only its active flag is set to false. However, the _validatorIndexes mapping maps validator addresses to array indices. If a validator is deactivated and later reactivated, its index remains the same. But if the contract were to ever remove entries from _validators (e.g., for cleanup), the _validatorIndexes mapping would become corrupted because it points to stale indices. While no such removal exists now, the design assumes the array is append-only. However, if future upgrades add a function to remove validators from _validators, the index mapping will break. This is a latent type system integrity flaw: the mapping between validator address and array index is fragile and not self-healing. The system relies on the invariant that array length equals number of validators ever created, but this is not enforced or documented as a design constraint.

extra_findings.title: Validation of Reward and Slashing Increments Uses Stale State, Enabling Reward Theft
extra_findings.description: The checkValidatorSanity function validates reward and slashing increments against previously stored values from validatorManager, but does not validate that these values are consistent with the current state of the validator. An attacker can front-run a legitimate validator update by submitting a maliciously low avgRewardAmount or avgSlashAmount, causing the system to accept a massive subsequent increase as 'within tolerance' because the baseline was artificially lowered. This allows an attacker to steal rewards by manipulating the baseline state before a legitimate update.

extra_findings.title: Reward and Slashing Accumulation Without Reset Causes Infinite Reward Theft
extra_findings.description: The updateValidatorMetrics function overwrites the reward and slashing fields entirely instead of accumulating them. This allows an operator to repeatedly update a validator's metrics with small positive reward values while setting slashing to zero, effectively stealing all previously earned rewards from the validator. Since the reward field is not additive, any prior reward accumulation is permanently lost on every update. This breaks the economic invariant that rewards should be cumulative over time, enabling an operator to drain all historical rewards from any validator by performing a series of malicious updates.

extra_findings.title: Mathematical Domain Violation in Reward/Slashing BPS Calculation
extra_findings.description: The contract calculates basis points (BPS) for slashing and rewards using Math.mulDiv(diff, BASIS_POINTS, avgBalance), but does not validate that avgBalance is non-zero before the division. Although a zero balance check exists earlier, it only returns 'Zero balance' without preventing the Math.mulDiv call in cases where avgBalance becomes zero due to race conditions or oracle manipulation between the check and the calculation. This leads to a division by zero, causing the transaction to revert, which is a denial-of-service vector for legitimate validators.

extra_findings.title: Score Change Tolerance Ignores Zero-Initial-State Edge Case
extra_findings.description: The score change checks (uptime, speed, integrity, self-stake) only perform tolerance validation if the previous score is greater than zero. If a validator has never been scored before (prevScore == 0), the check is skipped entirely. This allows an attacker to set an arbitrary high score (e.g., maxScoreBound) on a new validator without triggering any anomaly detection, even if the change is 100% from zero. This bypasses the entire score anomaly detection system for new validators.

extra_findings.title: Inconsistent Score Bound Enforcement for New Validators
extra_findings.description: The contract enforces maxScoreBound on incoming avgScore values, but does not enforce the same bound on the previous scores retrieved from validatorManager. This creates a logic gap: if a validator's previous score was set to 15000 (above maxScoreBound=10000) due to a bug or malicious update in validatorManager, the checkValidatorSanity function will still accept it as long as the delta is within scoreTolerance. This allows invalid historical scores to propagate and be treated as valid, corrupting the entire scoring system.

extra_findings.title: Rewards and Slashing Increment Checks Are Not Atomic with State Read
extra_findings.description: The function reads previous rewards and slashing values from validatorManager, then performs delta calculations. However, there is no mechanism to ensure that the state read and the subsequent checks are atomic. An attacker can front-run by triggering a reward or slashing update between the read and the check, causing the delta to appear artificially small or large. This enables manipulation of the tolerance thresholds by timing attacks, allowing invalid changes to pass or valid ones to be rejected.

extra_findings.title: Score Tolerance Comparison Uses Absolute Difference Without Normalization
extra_findings.description: The score change checks compute absolute differences (e.g., |avg - prev|) and compare them to scoreTolerance. However, scores are basis point values (0-10000), and a change of 1000 (10%) from a score of 1000 is a 100% relative change, while the same absolute change from 9000 is only ~11%. The tolerance is applied as an absolute delta, not a relative one, making the system highly asymmetric and exploitable. An attacker can make large relative changes from low scores without triggering alerts, while minor changes from high scores are flagged.

extra_findings.title: Validator Metrics Can Be Updated with Zero or Negative Reward/Slashing Values, Leading to Incorrect Reward Distribution
extra_findings.description: The updateValidatorMetrics function allows any operator to set reward and slashing values to zero or negative values without validation. Since these values are used in economic calculations (e.g., reward distribution, slashing penalties), setting them to zero or negative values can cause protocol insolvency or unfair distribution. For example, if an operator sets slashing = 0 for a validator who should be slashed, the protocol loses funds. Conversely, setting reward = 0 for a high-performing validator denies them earned rewards, undermining protocol incentives. The function validates only uptime, speed, integrity, and stake (0-10000), but ignores reward and slashing bounds entirely.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on getValidators and hasMetrics Enables Front-Running and MEV Exploitation
extra_findings.description: The functions getValidators() and hasMetrics() are public and view-only, but they expose the full list of active validators and their metrics status. An attacker can use this information to front-run validator updates or manipulate external systems that rely on validator activity (e.g., staking rewards, slashing triggers). Although these functions do not directly transfer funds, they expose critical economic state that enables MEV (Miner Extractable Value) attacks. For example, an attacker can observe a validator about to be slashed and trigger a withdrawal before the slash is applied, stealing funds. The interface design exposes sensitive state without access control, violating Pattern 4 (Access Control in Interfaces).

extra_findings.title: Validator Metrics Can Be Updated Before Initial Registration, Leading to State Inconsistency
extra_findings.description: The updateValidatorMetrics function calls _validators.add(validator) unconditionally after updating metrics, even if the validator has never been registered. This means a malicious operator can create a validator entry with arbitrary metrics without any prior onboarding or consent. This violates the logical invariant that validators must be registered before being tracked. An attacker can spam the system with fake validator addresses, bloating the _validators set and increasing gas costs for legitimate users. This is a state management issue (Pattern 6) because the state (_validators) is updated before any validation of validator legitimacy.

extra_findings.title: No Protection Against Reentrancy in updateValidatorMetrics Leading to Potential Reward Theft
extra_findings.description: The updateValidatorMetrics function performs state changes (updating validatorMetrics and adding to _validators) and then emits an event. If an external contract is called via a reward mechanism (e.g., a reward token that triggers on transfer or event), reentrancy could occur before the state is fully stabilized. Although no direct external call is made, if the reward value is used in a downstream system that calls back into this contract (e.g., a reward distributor that queries metrics and triggers a transfer), reentrancy could allow an attacker to manipulate state mid-execution. This is a control flow vulnerability (Pattern 6) where state is updated before external interactions are fully resolved.

extra_findings.title: MIN_UPDATE_INTERVAL Enforcement Is Bypassed by Setting lastUpdateTime to Zero
extra_findings.description: The function requires block.timestamp >= metrics.lastUpdateTime + MIN_UPDATE_INTERVAL. However, if a validator has never been updated, validatorMetrics[validator] defaults to all zeros, including lastUpdateTime = 0. Since 0 + 1 hour = 3600, and block.timestamp is typically > 3600 (after genesis), the check passes immediately. This allows an operator to update a new validator's metrics instantly upon first call, bypassing the intended 1-hour cooldown. This is a validation timing issue (Pattern 2) because the validation logic assumes non-zero initial state, but Solidity zero-initialization breaks the invariant. An attacker can spam updates to a new validator immediately, manipulating metrics before legitimate updates.

extra_findings.title: No Receiving Function Protection Allows Fund Theft via Unexpected ETH Deposits
extra_findings.description: The DefaultOracle contract has no receive() or fallback() function, but it can still receive ETH via direct transfers. Since the contract has no logic to handle or reject incoming ETH, any ETH sent to it becomes permanently locked. This is a critical issue because the contract is designed as an oracle for validator metrics and has no legitimate reason to hold ETH. Attackers can send ETH to the contract, and since there is no withdrawal mechanism for ETH, the funds are irrecoverable. This violates the principle that contracts should explicitly handle or reject native currency transfers.

extra_findings.title: Missing Validation of Reward and Slashing Non-Negativity
extra_findings.description: The updateValidatorMetrics function accepts reward and slashing values without validating they are non-negative. Since these are uint256 values, they cannot be negative by type, but the contract logic treats them as additive/subtractive amounts. If a malicious operator passes a value that underflows when subtracted (e.g., slashing > current balance), it can corrupt validator state. More critically, the contract assumes reward and slashing are absolute values to be added, but no bounds check ensures they are not absurdly large, leading to potential arithmetic overflow or inflation of validator rewards beyond intended limits.

extra_findings.title: State Commitment Before Update Interval Validation
extra_findings.description: The contract commits validator state (including lastUpdateTime) only after the update interval check, but the state is written unconditionally after the check. However, if the transaction reverts after the state write due to an external call or gas exhaustion, the lastUpdateTime is permanently advanced, preventing future updates even if the metrics update itself failed. This creates a denial-of-service vector: an attacker can trigger a revert after the timestamp update (e.g., by calling a malicious contract in a reward calculation) and lock the validator from future updates indefinitely.
